strings.text: The Canterville Ghost

An old English manor, an American family that does not believe in ghosts and offers theirs oil for his chains, and Sir Simon de Canterville, who murdered his wife and has not slept for three hundred years. You are Virginia, fifteen: will you stand with your laughing family, or beside the old murderer who asks you, once, to go with him through the wall? What is pity for one who did evil worth — and who pays for it?
A laughing family, a very tired ghost — and a girl of fifteen who has to choose where she stands.
after the story by Oscar Wilde
Oil for the Chains
At the crack of her door
“Good night, sir”
Let him pass
The paints
Leave him the box
Lock the paints away
Tell Washington
The First Night
Night, one o’clock. In the corridor — a clank of metal, footsteps, a groan. There is light under Virginia’s door.

The moonlit corridor. Down the middle of it walks an old man in fetters, his eyes burning like red coals. The door of the parents’ room opens: Mr Otis, in his dressing-gown and slippers, with a candle.
My dear sir, I really must insist on your oiling those chains. I have brought you a small bottle of the Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. It is said to be completely efficacious upon one application
He sets the bottle on the little table by the suit of armour and shuts his door.

The ghost stands still. Then he snatches up the bottle, dashes it on the floor and howls. From the twins’ door a pillow flies past his head. He backs away to the wall — past Virginia’s door, past the crack she is looking through.
Whisper: “Good night, sir”
Good night, sir
He stops dead and looks into the crack. His eyes go out — just an old man. He goes into the wall without answering.
He goes past without noticing the crack, and into the wall.
Only you see this. Sir Simon on his window-seat, rubbing the oil off his sleeve. He lays his ear to the wall: from below, the twins’ laughter.
Never, in a brilliant and uninterrupted career of three hundred years, had he been so grossly insulted
Oil. For me. For me, at whom the Dowager Duchess of Bolton…
He looks at the door.
“Good night”… She is mocking me
He decided you were mocking him.
The stain. We shall begin with the stain
Morning after morning. The stain is back in its place, bright red. Washington rubs it out; Papa locks the library and puts the key in his pocket; in the morning the stain is there again.
Sometimes it was a dull red, then it would be vermilion, then a rich purple
Breakfast at the window. The family bets on the colour.
A dollar on purple!
Two on vermilion!
The laws of Nature are not going to be suspended for the British aristocracy
Mrs Otis laughs. Virginia laughs with them —
— and looks at the floor.
Morning in the garden. Virginia at her easel, painting the old dry almond tree.
It does not flower. Not as long as I can remember
Virginia reaches for her red — the cakes of red and of vermilion are nearly gone, scraped out. She looks at the house.
Her reds are on the stain. Going to him herself is too soon: she has never spoken to him, and the Tapestry Chamber is the murderer’s room, where, Mrs Umney says, nobody goes.
Leave the open box by the library

In the evening she sets the open paint-box on the window-sill by the library doors. In the morning the box is in its place: the red, the vermilion and the purple scraped out clean. The stain is scarlet, fresh.
The box goes into the chest of drawers, the key under her pillow. In the night someone walks up and down outside her door for a long time; the chains clink, and fall silent.
In the morning the floor before the hearth is clean.
He takes my paints
Does he? Then we’ll be waiting for him
In the evening Washington begs the library key from Papa.
In the night, from the library —
For Ginny’s paints!
— a rattle of peas, a groan.
In the morning the stain is red, half painted, unfinished at one edge.
The Otis Ghost
The trap
Warn him
Watch with the boys
“Don’t,” to the boys
Breakfast. The reds have run out: the stain is emerald green.
The family roars with laughter; the twins collect their wagers.
Virginia looks at the stain, her lips trembling. She gets up from the table and goes out.
Breakfast. The floor is clean.
Boring
Our guest seems to have given up
Virginia looks at the clean floor.
Breakfast. The twins show how they fired:
Right in the knee!
Washington winks at Virginia; she does not wink back.
On the threshold, the young Duke of Cheshire, come to stay.
Virginia had twice raced old Lord Bilton on her pony round the park, and the young Duke fell in love with her on the spot — and stayed till the autumn
Shall we ride to the brook tomorrow?
Today

Evening; only you see this. Sir Simon before the old mirror, in his cloak — and in the mirror there is no one. He rehearses a howl and a gesture. Behind the wall, in the corridor, someone rustles and whispers; he howls louder.
Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl. Midnight. The corner of the corridor. The twins
He bows to the empty mirror.
Evening. At the corner of the corridor the twins and Washington are at work in whispers: a white sheet, a hollow turnip with a candle inside it, a kitchen knife, a placard:
“THE OTIS GHOST. The Only True and Original Spook. Beware of Imitations. All Others Are Counterfeit.”
Virginia is walking past.
Ginny, not a word to anyone! He walks here every night — he’ll run away from himself!
Come and watch. From behind the door
Tell the boys: “Don’t”
A quarter to midnight. She takes a candle and goes to the Tapestry Chamber.
The room is empty.
Sir Simon. It is Virginia. Don’t go round the corner tonight
Young lady. Ghosts do not change their routes
She leaves the candle-end on the window-sill.
Midnight. He comes down the corridor, stops at the corner, looks the glowing turnip over, runs a finger along the placard, snorts — and walks past. Behind the door the twins groan with vexation.
In the morning Washington looks at his sister.
Somebody told him
Midnight. She is behind the door with them. He comes round the corner — and before him stands a ghost with a glowing head and a knife.
A shriek. He backs away with his hands up and runs to his room.
The twins double up with laughter. Virginia laughs out loud —
— and claps her hand over her mouth.
He is old. Leave him alone
Ginny’s on the ghost’s side!
He killed his wife, Ginny
I know
She goes to her room. At midnight, through the wall — a shriek, and her brothers’ laughter.
Next morning the twins gallop down the corridor past the Tapestry Chamber:
Ginny’s on the ghost’s side! “He’s o-old!”
The days went by. Mrs Otis sent him a bottle of Doctor Dobell’s tincture for indigestion. The suit of armour came crashing down the stairs. Someone made a butter-slide on the floor of the corridor
Only you see this. He turns her candle-end in his fingers.
Warned. Me. As one helps an old woman across a puddle
And he hides the candle-end in his sleeve.
Only you see this. He sits before the hollow turnip with its placard — he took it from the corner at dawn — and shakes his chain. The chain does not ring.
He took to his bed. The stain appeared no more
Virginia sits at her easel and does not paint. Cecil sits down beside her on the grass, looks at the empty sheet and asks nothing.
Shall we ride?
Let’s
Night; the house has grown too quiet. Papa at his desk under the lamp, writing letters to London. Virginia in the doorway, in her nightgown.
Can’t sleep? Neither can I. Sit down
She sits on the window-sill with her sketchbook and draws him at his lamp.
Papa. If a person did something very bad — long, long ago — may one pity him?
Papa lays down his pen and thinks.
One may pity anyone, Ginny. Paying his debts — no
In the doorway, Washington with a candle: he saw the light.
Is this about our old man? Ginny, he killed his wife. And the butler shot himself because of him — Mrs Umney told us
He looks at her.
So it was you who told him
She does not answer — and does not look away.
About him again
He looks at her, not smiling.
Papa takes the drawing and looks at it.
It is like me. Let it stand here
He stands it against his inkstand. In the doorway, Mrs Otis in her shawl.
Your feet are like ice. Off to bed
Go. I’ll sit up a while. I can’t sleep anyway
The Tapestry Chamber
“Starved”
“Are you hungry? I have a sandwich”
“You killed her. Nothing else matters”
The wall
“I am not afraid”
“I’ll call Papa”
Autumn
Autumn. Virginia is back from a ride with Cecil, her habit torn on a hedge; she runs up the back stairs so that her mother will not see. The door of the Tapestry Chamber stands ajar.
He is at the window, watching the yellow leaves fall in the avenue, his head on his hand.
He hears her and turns; his eyes flare; up go his arms:
I am Red Reuben, or the Strangled…
She stands where she is. He lowers his arms and sits down.
He does not turn round.
Ah — the one who warns ghosts. I did not ask you to
And you laughed. Behind the door. I heard
“He’s old.” Your brothers shouted it under my door. Old. Hm
I am so sorry for you. But my brothers are going back to Eton soon. And then, if you behave yourself, no one will annoy you
Behave myself? I must rattle my chains, and groan through keyholes, and walk about at night. It is my only reason for existing
It is no reason at all for existing. And you have been very wicked. Mrs Umney told us you killed your wife
My wife was very plain, never had my ruffs properly starched, and knew nothing about cookery
Why, there was a buck I had shot in Hogley Woods, a magnificent pricket — and do you know how she had it sent up to table?
However, it is no matter now, for it is all over. And I don’t think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death
Though I did kill her
“Starved? Are you hungry? I have a sandwich”
Starved? Are you hungry? I have a sandwich
She takes a little parcel out of the pocket of her habit. He looks at the bread a long time — and takes it.
Thank you. I never eat anything now. But you are kind. Much nicer than the rest of your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family
You killed her. Nothing else matters
The cheap severity of abstract morality. Exactly like your horrid, rude, vulgar, dishonest family
She stamps her foot.
It is you who are rude and vulgar! And as for dishonest — who stole the paints out of my box?
I left them for you myself — and you made her green!
There was no red left. The emerald — yes, a mistake
To furbish up that ridiculous stain!
Well, really, where was I to get it? It is a very difficult thing to get real blood nowadays
Your brothers fired peas at me. At my knees, madam
I have not slept for three hundred years. I am so tired
Then why don’t you go to sleep?
Far away beyond the pine-woods there is a little garden. There the grass grows long and deep, there are the great white stars of the hemlock flower, and the nightingale sings all night long…
The tapestries darken; in the window, instead of the avenue, moonlit grass; a nightingale sings.
You mean the Garden of Death
To lie in the soft brown earth, and listen to silence. To have no yesterday, and no tomorrow
You can open its doors for me. For Love is always with you, and Love is stronger than Death
Have you ever read the old prophecy on the library window?

Oh, often. “When a golden girl can win prayer from out the lips of sin, when the barren almond bears, and a little child gives away its tears, then shall all the house be still.” I don’t know what it means
Weep with me for my sins — I have no tears. Pray with me for my soul — I have no faith. It will be dark there, and wicked voices will whisper in your ear. They will not harm you
Ginny! Supper!
The hunters on the tapestry stir; the wall behind him slowly parts, and beyond it there is darkness. He holds out his hand.
I shall not ask a second time
“I am not afraid. I will ask the Angel for you”
“No. I’ll call Papa”
I am not afraid. I will ask the Angel to have mercy on you
She takes his hand — a cold one.
Ginny!
The wall closes behind them; the tapestry sways, and hangs still.
No. I’ll call Papa
He lowers his hand.
He bows, as from the stage:
Call him. Let him bring the oil
He says nothing, and sits back down on the window-seat.
The wall closes slowly; out of the darkness beyond it something whispers:
Virginia…
She backs to the door, and runs downstairs.
The Garden of Death
The Last Night
Past the chair
Walk past Papa
Stay at the door
Wake Papa
Her name
“…and give rest to Lady Eleanore”
“Lord, let him sleep”
Evening by the fire; the whole family.
He asked me to go with him into the Garden of Death. Through the wall. To pray for him
You told us about him before. I believe you
How many times have you been to him, Ginny?
She does not answer. Papa touches her forehead — then looks at her longer, and stops smiling.
Papa takes a candle and climbs to the Tapestry Chamber: it is empty, the tapestry hangs still. He knocks politely on the wall with his knuckles.
Sir?
Silence.
We are going to London. Tomorrow morning, all of us
Mrs Otis nods.
And the ghost?
Nobody answers. Washington sits down beside her on the window-sill, without a word, turning his little black stick in his fingers.
Only you see this. The supper bell; Virginia is not there. Mrs Otis calls from the stairs; the twins run up and down the corridor.
Virginia! Ginny!
Washington with a lantern opens the Tapestry Chamber: empty; the tapestry hangs still.
He beats on the wall with his fist:
Give her back!
The wall is dead. He sits down under the tapestry with his lantern.
He looks round the empty room, and goes. In the window of the hall — his lantern down by the pond.
He does not knock. He sets his lantern on the floor and sits down under the tapestry — to wait.
In the library Papa takes her drawing from his desk and puts it in his inside pocket.
The gypsies were camped by the field
Hoofbeats in the yard: Papa and Cecil gallop off to the gypsy camp. Mrs Otis sits in the hall in her shawl, and does not get up.
At her door.
Promise me: never alone. Not to him, not after him
He holds out his hand.
I promise
He sets an armchair at her door and sits down in it with a book.
I’ll sit here. I can’t sleep anyway
You promised Papa: “Never alone.”
The moon, the long grass, the white stars of the hemlock, the old yew; a nightingale. Here he is without his irons — simpler, and older. They sit down in the grass.
He takes her parcel out of his sleeve, untouched, and lays it on the grass between them.
You said then: “You killed her. Nothing else matters.” Do you think so still?
Night. Papa is asleep in the armchair, the book on his knees.
At the far end of the corridor — Sir Simon in full array: fetters, cloak, eyes like coals. But he has carried his chains in his hand all the way from the corner.
For the first time in three hundred years Sir Simon walked down the corridor without a single sound
He comes barely visible, without his chains, a faint light.
He stops at her door. Virginia sees the light under it, and opens.
He bows.
I have come to take my leave. It is the custom
No one has offered me bread for three hundred years
Of everyone. Even of those who read me morals
And he goes off down the corridor, toward the Tapestry Chamber.
She stands on the threshold; his light is going away down the corridor.
She catches him up at the Tapestry Chamber.
I will come
He looks at her a long time.
You promised your father. I heard
The wall parts.
He stops, without turning round.
Good night, Miss Virginia
He does not stop.
His light vanishes into the wall. She shuts her door. Papa sleeps.
Papa wakes and sees the light at the end of the corridor. He gets up.
Sir. My daughter stays
The ghost makes a long, old-fashioned bow; he still holds his chains in his hand.
The ghost nods slightly.
He goes into the wall. Papa takes her by the hand.
The Garden: the moon, the long grass, the hemlock, the yew, the nightingale. They sit down in the grass.
The hall. The clock strikes — and with its last stroke the whole house falls silent: no wind, no creaking boards. Papa and Cecil have just come back with nothing.
The panel on the landing of the stairs opens with a crack; on the landing stands Virginia, pale, with a little casket in her hands.
Washington runs down from the Tapestry Chamber first and seizes both her hands.
She stands on the landing and does not come down till Papa climbs up to her himself.
Washington runs in with his lantern from the pond, last of all.
Washington comes from the Tapestry Chamber first, and stops two steps below her.
Mrs Otis rushes to her and takes her face in her hands.
How could you!
Papa, I have been with the ghost. He is dead. Come
He said her name
He was a very wicked man. I prayed for him

With candles — behind the panel, into the secret chamber. A skeleton chained to an iron ring, in the patch of moonlight from the little window; its fingers stretch toward an old trencher and ewer that stand just out of reach. Virginia kneels down.
The almond! The dry almond has blossomed!
In the moonlight the tree is white.
In the casket, old jewels — and on top of them, her candle-end.
In the casket, old jewels.
The clock strikes — and the whole house falls silent at once.
The silence wakes Papa: the armchair, the open door, the empty bed. He wakes no one.
He takes a candle to the Tapestry Chamber and knocks on the wall with his knuckles, as he did in the evening:
Sir. Ginny
Silence. He sets the candle on the floor and sits down facing the tapestry. The wall parts: Virginia, with the casket.
You promised
Yes
Show me
He does not give her his hand.

She leads him behind the tapestry, down a narrow passage in the wall, into the secret chamber — the one behind the panel on the stair landing: the skeleton, the trencher, the ewer. Papa stands in the doorway with his candle while she prays on her knees.
In the little window — the almond, in white blossom.
In the casket, jewels — and on top of them, her candle-end.
In the casket, jewels.
Darkness beyond the wall: only his pale light, and her face and hands in it. Shadows, wings, whispers:
Go back, little Virginia! Go back!
Do not listen
Pray with me. I do not remember the words. Of her — we will not speak
She prays aloud; he repeats after her, word for word.
Lord, have mercy on him — and give rest to Lady Eleanore
She begins with her, by name. He repeats — up to the name — and falls silent. He gets up and walks away from her to the edge of the grass.
Madam, I said: of her we will not speak. I am Sir Simon de Canterville, and I do not bargain at a graveside
He says nothing.
She waits, and prays no further. The nightingale falls silent. He looks a long time at the soft earth under the yew. Then, so quietly that it can hardly be heard:
Eleanore
There. Your father would be pleased: a bargain
He sits down again — further off than before — and repeats the prayer to the end: for her, then for himself. He does not look at Virginia. The nightingale sings no more.
Lord, let him sleep
She prays for him alone, as he asked. He repeats it like a child, and looks at her. The nightingale sings. Nobody speaks of Lady Eleanore.
“And a little child gives away its tears”: Virginia weeps — for him.
She takes his hand herself; he does not take it away, and does not raise his eyes from the earth.
He looks at her tears as at a miracle.
He takes a little casket out of his sleeve and lays it in her palm, without a word.
He lies down in the grass under the yew.
Farewell
Silence. He is gone.
The nightingale sings. He is gone.
Epilogue
The night after her return. Papa sets an armchair at her door and sits down in it with a book. He asks her nothing.
Mr Otis had slept badly before. From that night until they left Canterville he did not sleep at all

Four days later, at night. The churchyard under the old yew: torches, black plumes, the coffin on its trestles. Virginia lays on the coffin a cross of white almond blossom. The moon comes out from behind the clouds.
The whole family beside her; Washington with a torch; the twins silent.
She stands at the coffin alone; the family a step behind.
Morning, breakfast.
We shall stay four more days. A funeral
Whose, Hiram?
Ask Virginia
His. I went with him in the night. I promised Papa — and I went
Her mother puts down her cup and takes her hand. Washington gets up and goes out.
Virginia looks at the table.
Ginny?
She says nothing; Papa says nothing too. Her mother looks from one to the other.
At night she opens her door: no armchair; the corridor is empty.
Downstairs, in the library, the lamp: Papa is writing letters. The drawing that stood against his inkstand he has put away in a drawer of his desk.
The funeral, at night, under the yew. Virginia lays a cross of almond blossom on the coffin; Papa stands apart, with a candle.
The morning they leave. In the library, before the hearth, the stain again — fresh, scarlet; where he found the red, nobody knows. Washington takes out his little bottle.
Leave it. It is his house. At a valuation
The morning they leave. The floor is clean.
It has gone quiet. Quite quiet
Virginia leaves her sketch of the dry almond on the window-sill by the library: her paint-box has stood there since that night — she would not let it be cleared away. The sketch goes on top of it.
Virginia leaves her sketch of the dry almond on the window-sill by the library.
That morning her candle-end lay at her door. She takes it with her.
In the hall, Papa, buttoning his coat:
I believe I fell asleep in the night. Forgive me, Ginny
She says nothing, and takes his hand.
Papa is beside her all morning, and never takes his eyes off the windows of the Tapestry Chamber.
Years later. Virginia is a duchess; she is under the yew with Cecil.
You have never told me what happened to you that night
Don’t ask me, Cecil. He showed me what Life is, and what Death signifies, and why Love is stronger than both
You may keep your secret, as long as I have your heart
You have always had it
And you will tell our children some day, won’t you?
She blushes.
Moonlight on the flowering almond over the grave — and silence.
Moonlight on the flowering almond over the grave; the nightingale sings.
The Otises kept Canterville, and came there every summer
Her wedding. At the carriage.
I promise you, sir, she will write every week
Promise for yourself, Your Grace
He takes her hand — and lets it go first.
The carriage has gone. Papa, with a candle, goes into the Tapestry Chamber and sits down on the floor facing the tapestry, as on that night when he waited for her. The tapestry stirs no more. Quiet.
The porch; the carriages.
Papa gives her his hand at the carriage.
She sits between the twins, who are arguing about which of them will see London first.
She is the last to come down the steps, and turns to look at the windows of the Tapestry Chamber.
From above, from the windows of the Tapestry Chamber, a chain clinks — once. The twins fall silent; nobody laughs.
Nobody answers.
They say that at Canterville they still rattle chains at night, and the new owners buy lubricant
They say nothing has been heard at Canterville for a long time. Only the Tapestry Chamber is always cold
The carriages go down the avenue past the dry almond tree. It does not blossom.
No nightingale; quiet — only the torches crackle.
In the grove a nightingale begins to sing — the same as in the Garden.

In the morning, before the hearth in the library, an old brown stain has come through from under all the paints — a real one. Washington rubs it with Pinkerton’s Champion; it does not come off. He sits back on his heels and puts the stick in his pocket.
Put a rug over it
They unroll the rug. Virginia stands in the doorway, silent.
Pinkerton’s Champion
The face in the window
“There was someone. In the window”
Say nothing

Evening; rain lashes the painted window. The Otises come into the library with wet umbrellas: Mr Otis, Mrs Otis, Washington, the twins and Virginia. The old housekeeper, Mrs Umney, in black silk and a white cap, drops them a curtsey.
When Mr Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone told him he was doing a very foolish thing, as there was no doubt at all that the place was haunted
I will take the furniture and the ghost at a valuation
I am afraid something has been spilt there
Before the hearth, on the floor, a dark red stain.
Blood, madam. Lady Eleanore’s. Her own husband, Sir Simon, murdered her on this very spot. In fifteen hundred and seventy-five
The stain cannot be washed out. And his room is the Tapestry Chamber, upstairs. Nobody goes there
Washington is already on his knees by the hearth with a little black stick.
Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover. It will clean up anything
He rubs. The stain is gone. Lightning — and thunder through the whole house. Mrs Umney sinks into an armchair in a faint.
Hurrah!
Hurrah!
Everyone is laughing and fanning Mrs Umney. Virginia is looking at the dark window.
Lightning: in the glass, behind the family’s backs, an old face, its eyes like red coals. It is looking at the clean floor.
There was someone. In the window
Everyone turns round: in the window there is only rain.
A reflection, Ginny. Shall I take that out too?
The twins roar with laughter. Papa puts his hand on her shoulder.
It is only the storm, my dear
She looks at the window till Mrs Umney opens her eyes. The face is gone. She says nothing.

The Window

Six seconds of lightning: look at the dark window and touch nothing — and in the glass, behind the family’s backs, an old face with eyes like coals looks at the clean floor. Touched — the lightning goes out sooner, and she will say “There was someone… I think.” Alone in seeing it.
Everyone is laughing. The window is dark, and the rain lashes it.
The Door

Open her door a crack, slowly, so that it does not creak. Too quick — it creaks, and the ghost turns at the sound and looks into the crack with burning eyes. Fear and curiosity at one o’clock at night.
In the corridor: chains, steps, a groan. Light under her door.
The Sketch
Draw the brush along the old trunk of the almond, in one stroke. A slip — the trunk on the sketch is a blot, and stays so: in “The Stain” she leaves him that very sketch. Her own quiet work.
The old dry almond tree, the easel, a wet brush.
The Candle

Carry the candle down the dark corridor to his room so that it does not go out. It goes out — she whispers in the dark and he answers out of the dark; the stub stays all the same. Alone, at a quarter to midnight, to the murderer’s room.
A quarter to midnight. A candle, and the long corridor to the Tapestry Chamber.
The Portrait

Draw Papa at his lamp with a pencil, one line. A slip — the line goes askew; Papa: “My nose is longer, I believe,” laughs, and stands the drawing by his inkstand all the same. Two people who cannot sleep.
Papa at his desk under the lamp; the sketchbook on her knees.
The Nightingale

Ten seconds: touch nothing and listen — the tapestries darken, in the window, instead of the avenue, moonlit grass, and a nightingale sings. Touched — he breaks off: “You are not listening,” and finishes it shorter.
“Far away beyond the pine-woods there is a little garden…”
The Hand
Twelve seconds in the dark: hold his cold hand while the voices whisper “Go back!” The finger slips — her hand searches in the dark, and his finds hers by itself. Fear, and a hand that holds.
Darkness. Shapes, wings, whispers — and his pale hand.
Let Go
His hand grows weak in hers: hold it a moment, then let it go. Held too long — it slips out by itself. Letting him go to sleep.
His hand is growing weak.
The Word
Five seconds: lay her hand in Papa’s and hold it. Let go first — she takes her hand back, and Papa holds it a moment longer. A promise given with the hand.
Papa holds out his hand: “Promise.”
On Tiptoe
Past the chair, past the sleeping face, on tiptoe, eight seconds. A board creaks — Papa mutters “Ginny?..” and sleeps on. A word broken quietly.
Papa asleep in the chair, the book on his knees. His light going down the corridor.
The Threshold
Six seconds on the threshold: touch nothing while his light goes away. Touched — she takes half a step over the threshold and stops; he does not turn. Staying.
His light is going away down the corridor.
The Shoulder
Reach slowly for Papa’s shoulder, five seconds. Too sharp — Papa starts up, the book falls. Calling him to stand beside her.
Papa asleep in the chair at her door.
narrator
Virginia
Sir Simon
Mr Otis
Washington
Mrs Otis
a twin
the other twin
Mrs Umney
voices
Cecil
In truth: the corridor upstairs — long, in moonlit windows; a suit of armour on its stand and a little table beside it; the bedroom doors; at its end, the door of the Tapestry Chamber.
In truth: the dark behind the wall — nothing but his pale light, and her face and hands in it.
In truth: the secret chamber — low, of stone; an iron ring in the wall, a chain, a skeleton; an old trencher and ewer just out of its reach; the moon through a little window.
In truth: the garden by the house — the old dry almond tree, the lawn, the avenue to the gates; beyond the railings, the churchyard and its old yew.
In truth: the hall — the great staircase and its landing, the clock, an armchair at the foot of the stairs, the window onto the pond, the front door.
plays

Virginia: shares — keeps it to herself. Whether she brings what she sees and thinks to her family, to their faces, or carries it alone.
You told them about the face in the window. They laughed.
You kept the face in the window to yourself.
You wished him good night.
You left him your paints. By morning there was no red left in the box.
You locked your paints away. All night someone walked up and down by your door.
You told Washington. In the night they fired peas in the library.
You warned him. Washington looked at you: “Somebody told him.”
You watched with your brothers — and laughed out loud.
You said “Leave him alone” to your brothers’ faces. He got his fright all the same.
You gave him bread. He called you kind, and your family vulgar.
“You killed her. Nothing else matters.” He called it cheap morality.
You took his hand. Downstairs they were calling you to supper.
You said you would call Papa. He did not ask again.
You named her in the prayer. The nightingale sang no more.
You prayed for him alone. Nobody said her name.
You walked past the chair. Your word to Papa is broken.
You stayed at the door. He went, and nobody but you knows.
You woke Papa. Sir Simon’s farewell was his: “My daughter stays.”
